title: How to Talk to Parents About Fall Progress
summary: A practical guide for IB teachers discussing September-November progress with parents using evidence, careful forecasts, and realistic next steps.
body_markdown:
For an **IB teacher in the fall term** , the safest way to talk to parents about progress is to explain what current evidence shows, identify what remains uncertain, and agree on observable next steps. Avoid presenting an early report, positive trend, or predicted grade as a guaranteed final outcome.


This distinction is especially important from September to November. DP1 students are adjusting to IB expectations, while DP2 students may be completing coursework, receiving predictions, and applying to universities. Parents should leave the conversation understanding the student's present level, the evidence behind that judgment, and what improvement would look like.


### Why fall progress requires careful language


Fall evidence is informative but incomplete. A student may have completed only a few tests, essays, practical tasks, oral activities, or coursework checkpoints, none of which necessarily represents the full range of final assessment demands.


The IB describes Diploma Programme assessment as **criterion-related** , meaning performance is judged against defined standards rather than class rank. Its[Diploma Programme grade descriptors](https://ibo.org/contentassets/0b0b7a097ca2498ea50a9e41d9e1d1cf/dp-grade-descriptors-en.pdf) support formative assessment, reporting, and grade prediction.


Term Meaning Appropriate wording


**Current attainment** The standard shown in completed work “Recent essays are currently consistent with this descriptor.”


**Progress** Change across comparable evidence “Analysis has become more precise across the last three tasks.”


**Prediction** A professional forecast of likely performance “This is our best estimate from the available evidence, not a guarantee.”


Parents may hear “on track” as a promise. Define its conditions: “On track if the student sustains this standard, meets coursework deadlines, and transfers these skills to timed assessments.”


### Prepare an evidence-based progress snapshot


Select a small body of representative evidence rather than reading every mark. The[IB assessment overview](https://ibo.org/programmes/diploma-programme/assessment-and-exams/) explains that assessment includes internal and external components and tests skills such as analysis, argument, application, and problem-solving. Evidence should therefore extend beyond factual recall.


Prepare five points:


- one demonstrated strength
- one recurring limitation linked to criteria or assessment objectives
- the pattern across comparable recent work
- one relevant coursework or organizational concern
- one action to review by a stated date


Assessment conditions matter. A lower mark on a closed-book examination than on untimed homework does not automatically indicate declining attainment. Effort, attendance, and punctuality provide useful context, but they are not direct proof of an IB grade.


Digital practice data should also remain a **practice indicator** , not formal assessment evidence. RevisionDojo's guide to[tracking IB progress without spreadsheets](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-ib-teachers-can-track-student-progress-without-spreadsheets) can reveal topic-level patterns, but those patterns should supplement marked work and teacher judgment.


### Structure the parent conversation


### Establish the scope and judgment


Begin by identifying the period and evidence covered: “This update includes work completed from September through mid-October, including two timed responses and the first coursework checkpoint.” This prevents an interim update from being mistaken for a judgment on the complete Diploma Programme.


Then state the current evaluation clearly. “The student is working securely at the level described here” is more useful than “Things seem fine.” Connect the conclusion to a rubric, markscheme, grade descriptor, or repeated pattern.


### Explain the evidence and uncertainty


Show why the judgment was reached. For example: “Knowledge is generally secure, but marks are being lost because evaluation is brief and conclusions are not consistently supported.” This explains why a strong homework average may coexist with a cautious forecast.


State what has not yet been tested, such as cumulative knowledge, full examination timing, oral performance, independent coursework, or the ability to sustain recent improvement. Useful wording includes:


- “We do not yet have enough cumulative evidence for a firm longer-term judgment.”
- “The direction is encouraging, but the pattern must continue across several tasks.”
- “This estimate may change when broader, more exam-like evidence becomes available.”


### Finish with actions and a review date


Agree on no more than two high-value actions. Specify what the student will do, what support the teacher will provide, and when the evidence will be reviewed.


For example: “Before the November assessment, the student will complete two timed data-response sets, classify lost marks, and revisit the weakest topic. We will compare the result with the September baseline.” RevisionDojo's[Questionbank and progress tools for schools](https://www.revisiondojo.com/schools) can support targeted practice when aligned with the taught course.


### Discuss predicted grades without making promises


The IB defines a **predicted grade** as the teacher's prediction of the grade a candidate is expected to achieve, based on available evidence and knowledge of IB standards. Its guidance on[IB assessment and predicted grades](https://ibo.org/university-admission/discover-why-ib-students-succeed/ib-student-assessment/) says predictions should be as accurate as possible, without systematic over-prediction or under-prediction.


A prediction is not a reward for effort, a negotiable university target, or the final grade. When discussing one, clarify:


- whether it is a working forecast, report grade, university prediction, or IB submission
- which evidence and assessment formats were included
- when the school reviews or finalizes predictions
- which school policy governs questions or appeals


The[IB Programme standards and practices](https://www.ibo.org/globalassets/new-structure/become-an-ib-school/pdfs/programme-standards-and-practices-2020-en.pdf) emphasizes open communication and consistent, fair processes. Teachers should follow school assessment policy rather than promise that one improved test will change a prediction. Families needing further explanation can consult RevisionDojo's guide to[how IB predicted grades work](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/when-and-how-are-predicted-grades-predicted-in-ib-a-clear-guide-for-students-and-parents) .


### Adjust the message for DP1 and DP2


In early DP1, emphasize adaptation to subject demands, foundational skills, and response to feedback. There is usually too little evidence for a confident final-grade forecast, especially before cumulative or fully timed assessments.


DP2 conversations may have greater consequences because predictions, references, coursework, the Extended Essay, TOK, and university applications can converge. Be direct about evidence and deadlines, but never imply that meeting an entry requirement guarantees admission or that a prediction guarantees the final IB result. RevisionDojo's[IB parent checklist from DP1 to results](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-parent-checklist-by-year) helps families distinguish academic priorities from administrative deadlines.


### Avoid common communication mistakes


Do not lead with a number, confuse effort with attainment, or overreact to one result. Explain whether a task was representative, timed, cumulative, and independently completed before drawing conclusions.


Replace “They need to work harder” with a subject-specific action such as “They need to link each conclusion explicitly to evidence.” Limit next steps to one academic skill and one organizational priority. Where school procedures permit, include the student's reflection so everyone hears the same expectations.


When parents request certainty, use a calm script:


> “I understand why the likely outcome matters. The strongest current evidence is X, while Y is limiting performance. We have not assessed Z under full conditions, so I cannot guarantee a final grade. The next step is A, and we will review the evidence after B.”


If the dispute concerns procedure rather than classroom evidence, involve the DP coordinator. The[2026 DP general regulations](https://www.ibo.org/globalassets/new-structure/become-an-ib-school/pdfs/dp-2026-general-regulations.pdf) identify the coordinator as the intermediary for questions about programme administration and implementation.


### Conclusion


Effective fall progress conversations separate **current attainment** , **progress** , and **prediction** . They use representative evidence, acknowledge uncertainty, and conclude with limited actions and a review date.


RevisionDojo can support follow-up through Questionbank practice, Study Notes, Mock Exams, and Jojo AI. These tools are most useful when they form part of an evidence-based plan guided by teacher feedback and school policy.
